claim: Lydian gold staters of the Croesus era (c. 560-546 BCE) are the earliest known coins struck in pure gold, following the earlier electrum coins of the same kingdom.
object: Gold stater with confronted foreparts of lion and bull, excavated at Sardis 13 April 1922
photo_licence: Public Domain / Met Open Access (page shows 'Public Domain' + Download Image)
visible_payoff: Lion and bull foreparts facing each other, stamped on the coin face; the very first 'brand mark' on money.
why_now: Skara Brae/Goodwill-statue/oldest-X outliers reward concrete, holdable objects; money/debt is a proven channel theme (Ea-nasir, Kushim).
frame0: A Lydian mint worker mid-swing, hammer coming down on a glowing gold blank held on an anvil, sparks flying.
confidence: medium (Met page does not itself say 'earliest'; claim wording must stay 'earliest known pure-gold coinage'; licence verified)

claim: A c. 1900 BCE Egyptian school writing board bearing a student's copied model letter corrected by a teacher in red ink is among the earliest surviving examples of marked homework.
photo_licence: Public Domain / Met Open Access (page shows 'Public Domain' + Download Image)
visible_payoff: Red-ink teacher corrections over the student's many spelling mistakes, plus faint traces of earlier erased writing on the left.
why_now: School/complaint/mundane-life stories mirror the Ea-nasir style that already works; short, relatable, 'ancient people were like us' hook.
frame0: A teenage scribe-student wincing as a teacher's brush drags a red line across his board.
confidence: medium-low (Met describes the corrections but does not say 'earliest'; use 'among the oldest surviving' wording only if a scholarly source is added; licence verified)
